slides.title: What XSS is
slides.summary: XSS happens when attacker-controlled data ends up running as code in your page, with all of your origin's power.
body: Cross-site scripting is the most common frontend vulnerability. The attacker gets the browser to treat their text as HTML or JavaScript inside your page.
Once their script runs, it is your app as far as the browser is concerned. It can:

ul: read the page, including personal data and CSRF tokens;
read localStorage and any token you keep there;
make authenticated requests as the user (change email, transfer money);
rewrite the page to show a fake login form.

body: <mark>Any place where data becomes markup or code is a possible XSS sink.</mark>

steps.caption: The payload is stored as ordinary text.
The developer used innerHTML to support bold text.
The image fails to load, so its error handler runs.
Every reader of the comment is now compromised.

slides.title: Three kinds of XSS
slides.summary: Stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS differ in where the payload lives, but the fix is the same: never let data become code.

ul: Stored: the payload is saved in your database (a comment, a profile name) and served to every viewer.
Reflected: the payload is in the request, usually the URL, and the server echoes it back into the page.
DOM-based: the payload never reaches the server. Client code reads it from location, postMessage or storage and writes it into the DOM.

body: Single-page apps mostly face DOM-based XSS, because the client does the rendering.

body.note: Server-side scanners often can't see DOM XSS, because the dangerous flow happens entirely in the browser.

slides.title: Encode for the context
slides.summary: The right escaping depends on where the data lands: HTML text, an attribute, a URL or a script.
body: The main defence is output encoding: turn special characters into harmless text for the context the data is written into.

ul: Attributes: always quote them and escape quotes; never build event-handler attributes from data.
URLs: allow only https:, http: and mailto:. A javascript: URL in an href runs code on click.
Inside <script>: don't. Pass data with JSON in a data attribute or a type="application/json" block.

body: <mark>Frameworks escape text bindings for you. XSS in modern apps almost always comes through an escape hatch.</mark>

viz.html: Search your codebase for the right-hand column. Each hit needs a reason and a review.

slides.title: When you must render HTML
slides.summary: Sanitize with a maintained library, then lock the sinks down with Trusted Types and a CSP.
body: Rich text editors, Markdown and CMS content need real HTML. Don't write your own filter: regex-based blocklists are bypassed all the time.

ul: Sanitize with a maintained library such as DOMPurify, or Angular's built-in sanitizer, using an allowlist of tags and attributes.
Sanitize as late as possible, just before rendering, so nothing changes the HTML afterwards.
Turn on Trusted Types so the browser rejects plain strings passed to innerHTML and other sinks.
Add a strict CSP so that even if a payload gets through, inline scripts don't run.

body.text: A CSP feature: with require-trusted-types-for 'script', DOM sinks only accept typed objects created by a policy you define. Every risky write then goes through one reviewed function. Angular supports it out of the box.
